plan.topic: GLP-1 users and nail detachment (onycholysis): 39% vs 9% in comparable non-users, the first controlled study (575 users vs 1,329 controls, EADV 2026)
plan.angle: Title: 'Can GLP-1 Drugs Like Ozempic Affect Your Nails? 39% vs 9% Self-Reported #shorts'. Answer within 10 seconds: 'A new survey-style study found more nail problems in people taking GLP-1s, but it can't show the drug causes them.' On screen: '575 GLP-1 users vs 1,329 non-users with T2D/obesity · self-reported · cross-sectional · congress abstract, not peer-reviewed · ~2–3× after adjustment'. Add a one-line definition of onycholysis, gentle nail-care habits with no supplement claims, when to see a clinician, and the exact prescriber line. Don't tell anyone to stop their medicine.
plan.working_title: Can Ozempic (Semaglutide) Affect Your Nails? 39% vs 9% in First Controlled Study #shorts
plan.why: A brand-new controlled number on a complaint that already circulates on Reddit and TikTok. Creators haven't covered it yet, and it extends our hair-loss piece (top 2 of 5 long-forms). | fact-check: Verified: EADV Congress 2026, 575 GLP-1 RA users vs 1,329 people with T2D and/or obesity who had never used them, recruited in France, the US, Brazil and Mexico. Nail detachment was 39% vs 9% and discoloration 46% vs 17%. The study was cross-sectional, with patient-reported symptoms, and is a congress abstract that hasn't been peer-reviewed. After adjustment the gap shrank to about 2–3× more frequent. The authors say it cannot establish causation. Problems: (1) The title leads with Ozempic/semaglutide, but the study covered GLP-1 RA users in general, and the specific drugs aren't reported. This breaks the brand rule. (2) 'First controlled study' is the press-release framing. Say 'described by researchers as the first controlled study', or drop it. (3) The raw 39% vs 9% must sit next to 'about 2–3× after adjustment'. Don't use the press 'over 4x higher risk' wording. These are self-reported prevalence figures, not risk. (4) Don't imply that protein prevents nail changes. Habits are general nail care and a balanced diet, not a fix. Add the red flags: pain, signs of infection, or changes in only one nail mean see a GP or dermatologist. Keep the tone reassuring, not alarming.

package.title: GLP-1 Nail Lifting: 39% vs 9%, ~2–3x After Adjusting #shorts
package.description:
A new controlled study of 575 GLP-1 users vs 1,329 non-users (all with type 2 diabetes, obesity or both) found nail detachment (onycholysis) reported in 39% vs 9%: about 2–3x more common after adjusting for other skin conditions and nutrient deficiencies. It's self-reported, about half had nail problems before starting, and it was presented at a conference with no journal paper yet as of Sept 2026. Researchers say it's usually harmless and not a reason to stop treatment on your own.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.hook_pattern: The opener is a search-style question with a 'you' stake ("Nails lifting on a GLP-1?"). A plain answer lands by about 5s: more nail problems were reported, but the cause isn't proven. Next come the population (drugs not named) and the raw 39% vs 9%, then a one-line definition. At about 30s, 'The catch' re-hooks with the ~2–3× adjusted figure and what it was adjusted for. A short caveats list follows: self-reported, one snapshot, about half had nail problems before starting, and conference data with no journal paper as of September 2026. Then come gentle nail care and the red flags from NHS and DermNet. It closes on the researchers' reassurance (usually harmless, not a reason to stop on your own) and the exact prescriber line.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the script against both EADV release versions (Medical Xpress and Mirage News), DermNet and the NHS. Most of it is accurate and well hedged. The numbers match the release: 575 users vs 1,329 controls, 39% vs 9% nail detachment, about 2–3× after adjustment, cross-sectional and self-reported, and about half had nail problems before starting. The release names no specific drugs. Both the conference date and the lack of a journal paper check out. The researcher quote is real: "usually benign... not a reason to stop an effective treatment on one's own initiative". The nail-care tips and red flags match DermNet and the NHS.

There's one scope error that needs fixing. s3 says "all" participants had type 2 diabetes and/or obesity, but the source only describes the 1,329 controls that way. Everything else is minor wording.

issues.claim: 575 GLP-1 users versus 1,329 non-users, all with type 2 diabetes, obesity or both.
issues.problem: Scope error. Both release versions say: 'Researchers compared 575 GLP-1 receptor agonist users with 1,329 people with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity who had never taken the drugs.' Only the controls are described as having T2D and/or obesity. The users' conditions aren't stated, so 'all' goes further than the source.
issues.fix: 575 GLP-1 users versus 1,329 non-users with type 2 diabetes, obesity or both. Drugs weren't named. Nail lifting: 39% versus 9%.

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: The fact-checker found a major scope error that is still unfixed. The narration and every caption (YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Threads) say "all" participants had type 2 diabetes, obesity or both, but the source only describes the 1,329 non-users that way. That makes the 39% vs 9% comparison look more like-for-like than the evidence shows. Smaller issues are also open: the script says "harmless" where the source says "benign", and a sound effect (cue i=83) is almost silent and may need re-rendering.

notes: The stat pill reads '39% vs 9%' but the caption spells it out as '39% VERSUS 9%.' — inconsistent number/format between pill and caption, which the style rules call out to avoid.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right at the top of the window in pauses (-11 vs ~-14 target) so I trimmed overall music -1.5 dB (0.85×), which lands pauses near -12.5 dB and speech-under at ~-14.9 dB — both inside target without losing presence. Trimmed a handful of cues that read 2–4 dB hot during speech (i=2,3,33,35,39,55) back toward -16/-17 dB so they stay felt-not-heard; dropped one redundant blip (i=67) in the second rapid chip run at 65–68s since three blips already carry that beat. The i=83 swell before the "Usually harmless" reveal is anomalously near-silent (-52 dB) — likely an envelope/clipping glitch — so I pushed its gain to the 1.5 cap, but it may need a re-render rather than a gain fix. Added three bespoke accents: a soft paper/clinical-data flutter under the "575 vs 1,329" label, a gentle reassuring chime under "Usually harmless," and a warm closing bell under the final CTA, all mixed low so they support rather than compete with the voice. Left the big reveal cluster at 22.7s (39% vs 9%) and the onycholysis reveal at 27.3s as-is since those are intentional accented moments.
